clinicalPearls: A rare condition of marked dilatation of the trachea and main bronchi (tracheobronchomegaly) due to atrophy or deficiency of elastic and smooth-muscle tissue in the airway wall
Redundant airway mucosa herniates between cartilage rings, producing characteristic tracheal diverticulosis and a corrugated appearance
Presents typically in middle-aged men with chronic productive cough, recurrent lower respiratory infections, and bronchiectasis
The enlarged, flaccid airways collapse on expiration and impair secretion clearance, predisposing to infection and bronchiectasis
Diagnosis rests on measuring tracheal and bronchial diameters on CT above defined thresholds, alongside the typical clinical picture
Bronchoscopy shows a widened, flaccid airway with mucosal outpouchings between cartilaginous rings
Management is supportive, centred on airway clearance, treatment of infections, and management of associated bronchiectasis
reference.pathophysiology: Mounier-Kuhn syndrome is characterised by atrophy or congenital deficiency of the elastic fibres and smooth muscle of the tracheal and bronchial walls, which causes progressive dilatation of these large airways. The weakened wall allows the mucous membrane to bulge outward between the cartilage rings, forming diverticula and giving a scalloped contour, and the flaccid airway collapses excessively during expiration and coughing. This dynamic collapse and enlargement impair the effectiveness of cough and mucociliary clearance, leading to retained secretions, recurrent infection, and secondary bronchiectasis. Most cases are considered congenital, and associations with connective tissue disorders have been described.
additionalDifferentials: Tracheal dilatation from traction by pulmonary fibrosis
Ehlers-Danlos or other connective tissue disorders affecting the airway
additionalInvestigations: CT of the thorax measuring tracheal and main bronchial diameters and demonstrating diverticulosis
Dynamic expiratory imaging or bronchoscopy to assess airway collapse
Bronchoscopy showing the widened flaccid airway and mucosal outpouchings
Pulmonary function tests including flow-volume loops
Assessment for associated bronchiectasis and connective tissue disease
redFlags: Recurrent severe pneumonia or respiratory failure from secretion retention
Massive or extensive bronchiectasis with declining lung function
Haemoptysis requiring evaluation in the context of bronchiectasis
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; some patients remain relatively stable with airway clearance and prompt treatment of infections, while others develop progressive bronchiectasis and respiratory impairment, and prognosis is largely determined by the extent of secondary lung damage.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis and attributing recurrent infection to ordinary bronchiectasis without noting the megatrachea
Failing to measure airway diameters on CT
Missing the diagnostic clue of tracheal diverticulosis and a corrugated airway
Not addressing dynamic airway collapse contributing to poor secretion clearance
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Prioritise airway clearance with chest physiotherapy, postural drainage and mucolytics or nebulised hypertonic saline to overcome poor cough and secretion retention
Give targeted antibiotics for recurrent lower respiratory infections, directed by sputum culture
Immunise against influenza and pneumococcal disease and support smoking cessation
Treat associated bronchiectasis and use bronchodilators alongside pulmonary rehabilitation
Trial continuous positive airway pressure to splint the collapsing large airways, reserving tracheobronchial stenting or reconstructive surgery for selected refractory cases
Screen for and manage any associated connective tissue disorder
Monitor pulmonary function and escalate to non-invasive ventilation, considering lung transplantation in end-stage respiratory failure
